name: notalgia paraesthetica
aliases: posterior ramus sensory neuropathy of the back

clinicalPearls: A sensory neuropathy of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves presenting as a localised, chronically itchy patch on the upper or mid back, usually just medial to the scapula.
The hallmark is a well-circumscribed area of pruritus often accompanied by burning, tingling or a localised hyperpigmented patch from chronic rubbing and scratching.
The hyperpigmentation is secondary to chronic friction and postinflammatory change rather than a primary pigmentary disorder, and biopsy may show amyloid deposition.
The distribution corresponds to the posterior rami of thoracic dermatomes, most often in the T2 to T6 range.
Symptoms may improve transiently with cooling or capsaicin and are typically resistant to conventional antihistamines, reflecting the neuropathic mechanism.
An association with degenerative changes of the thoracic spine and with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A has been described.
It is closely analogous to brachioradial pruritus, which affects the dorsolateral forearm through a comparable neuropathic mechanism.
Diagnosis is clinical; the key is to recognise the neuropathic nature and avoid an exhaustive search for primary skin disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Notalgia paraesthetica is attributed to dysfunction of the posterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves supplying sensation to the paravertebral skin of the back. Proposed mechanisms include entrapment or compression of these cutaneous nerve branches as they pass through the paraspinal musculature at a near right angle, and irritation associated with degenerative thoracic spine disease. The resulting neuropathic itch and dysaesthesia provoke chronic rubbing and scratching, which produce the characteristic hyperpigmented, sometimes lichenified patch; histology may reveal dermal amyloid deposition thought to be secondary to the chronic friction rather than a primary amyloidosis.
additionalDifferentials: tinea or other localised cutaneous infection
thoracic radiculopathy or herpes zoster-related neuropathic itch
cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting as a persistent patch
additionalInvestigations: clinical examination mapping the itch to a thoracic dermatomal distribution
thoracic spine imaging to assess degenerative or structural change when clinically indicated
skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude amyloid and other dermatoses
screening for features of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A in selected patients
dermoscopy to characterise the pigmented patch
assessment of posture and musculoskeletal contributors
review for coexisting neuropathic itch syndromes such as brachioradial pruritus
redFlags: an evolving, indurated or ulcerated plaque that could represent cutaneous malignancy
associated neurological deficit or radicular pain suggesting significant spinal pathology
features suggesting multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A such as relevant family history or endocrine symptoms
rapidly spreading or systemic symptoms inconsistent with a localised neuropathic itch
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but typically chronic and relapsing, with symptoms that can be controlled but often persist over years. Treatment directed at the neuropathic mechanism and reduction of scratching improves symptoms and the associated pigmentation.
pitfalls: treating the hyperpigmented patch as a primary pigmentary or infective dermatosis and missing the neuropathic cause
prescribing sedating antihistamines that are ineffective for neuropathic itch
overlooking an association with thoracic spine disease or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A
attributing a persistent solitary patch to notalgia without considering cutaneous lymphoma when atypical
management: Topical capsaicin to deplete substance P and relieve the neuropathic itch
Oral neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants when topical measures are insufficient, reflecting the neuropathic mechanism
Topical local anaesthetics and cooling for symptomatic relief, with measures to interrupt the itch-scratch cycle that drives hyperpigmentation
Physiotherapy, posture correction and treatment of underlying degenerative thoracic spine disease
Local injection therapy such as botulinum toxin in refractory cases
Screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A in selected patients with suggestive features
